background.definition: UTI is a common bacterial infection of the urinary tract in children. It is an important cause of acute morbidity and long-term complications.

list.listitem: By the age of 7, 1.7% of boys and 8.4% of girls will have suffered one UTI.
In infants younger than 60 days with a temperature above 38°C, the prevalence is 9%.
The overall prevalence in febrile infants younger than 12 months and girls younger than 2 years presenting to the emergency room is 3.3%.
The prevalence in febrile children <2 years is 5%.
In neonates, infection is usually due to hematogenous spread or bacteremia.
UTIs beyond the newborn period are due to an ascending infection.
Colonization of the periurethral area with enteric pathogens is the initial step.
Bacteria then attach to receptors on the epithelial cells.
Virulence factors such as the pili in E. coli facilitate ascension up to the kidney.
A meta-analysis of 12 studies found that routine circumcision does not reduce UTI enough to justify the complications of surgery. B
Antibiotic prophylaxis does not decrease the risk of recurrent UTI in children younger than 6 years of age; data are lacking regarding children with grade 5 VUR. B
There is some evidence that cranberry juice, D-mannose, and probiotics are effective in reducing recurrent UTIs in women. This is not yet proven for children.
A study of 140 women with frequents UTIs (>3/year) found that increasing water intake by 1.5 L/d decreased UTI frequency (1.7 vs. 3.2 UTIs/y; p <0.001). This is not yet proven for children.
A meta-analysis of 12 studies and 400,000 boys showed that routine circumcision does not reduce UTI enough to justify the complications of surgery.
Relief of constipation and voiding dysfunction will decrease recurrences.

Antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with decreased risk of recurrent febrile UTI in children 2 months to 7 years of age. However, conclusions cannot be drawn about children with grade 5 VUR, as there were only 5 children (2 months-2 years) in that category. An RCT of 607 children with VUR may challenge these earlier findings as this 2-year study found that antibiotic prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prevented recurrent UTIs by 50% (HR: 0.50; 95% CI: 0.34-0.74), and was particularly effective in children whose index UTI was a febrile UTI (HR: 0.41; 95% CI: 0.26-0.64) and in those with baseline bladder and bowel dysfunction (HR: 0.21; 95% CI: 0.08-0.58). There was no difference in occurence of renal scarring.
Antibiotic exposure is associated with treatment resistant pathogens.
Absence of frequency, urgency, nocturia or history of previous UTI are good indicators that a child does not have a UTI.C
Positive dipstick for both leukocyte esterase and nitrite and microscopic positivity for both pyuria and bacteriuria are most useful to rule in disease. C
Negative dipstick for both LE and nitrite or microscopy negative for both pyuria and bacteriuria rule out the disease. C

Diagnosis of UTI requires both a urinalysis that suggests infection (pyuria and/or bacteriuria) and at least 50,000 cfu/ml of a uropathogen on urine culture obtained through clean catch, suprapubic aspiration, or catheterization. C
Bladder and kidney ultrasound is recommended for first febrile UTI in children younger than 2 years. C

list.listitem: In general, the absence of frequency, urgency, nocturia, and previous UTI reduces the likelihood of UTI. The best predictors of UTI in children are frequency, offensive urine odor, urgency, and nocturia.
The presence of UTI should be considered in any child younger than 2 years of age with unexplained fever. For children 2 to 24 months, the UTI prevalence is 5% for fever without obvious source.

For girls (2-24 months), risk factors for UTI are: white race, age <12 months, temperature 39°C or higher, fever for 2 or more days, and absence of another source of infection. For febrile female infants with 1 or fewer risk factors, the probability of UTI is 1% or lower; with 2 or fewer risk factors, the probability of UTI is 2% or lower.

For boys (2-24 months), risk factors for UTI are: nonblack race, temperature 39°C or higher, fever for more than 24 hours, and absence of another source of infection. For uncircumcised febrile male infants, the probability of UTI is >2%. For circumcised febrile male infants with 2 or fewer risk factors, the probability of UTI is 1% or lower; with 3 or fewer risk factors, the probabilty of UTI is 2% or lower.
Newborns: jaundice, sepsis, failure to thrive, vomiting, and fever are clinical signs and symptoms of UTI.
Infants and preschoolers: diarrhea, failure to thrive, vomiting, fever, abdominal and flank pain, new-onset incontinence, dysuria, and urgency (preschoolers only) are clinical symptoms.
School age: vomiting, fever, abdominal and flank pain, new-onset incontinence, dysuria, urgency, and frequency are symptoms.
A urine specimen in a child unable to produce a clean catch urine should be obtained via suprapubic aspiration (SPA) or transurethral catheterization.

In infants younger than 3 months of age, a noninvasive method of collecting clean-catch urine will be effective more than half the time: Feed the infant for 20 minutes; clean the genital area; parent holds the infant under armpits with legs dangling in males and hips flexed in females, exposing genital area to air, alternately gently tap in suprapubic region (100 taps/minute for 30 seconds) followed by lumbar paravertebral massage for 30 seconds, for a maximum of 5 minutes. Contamination will occur in approximately 1 in 6 samples. In infants 1 to 12 months, an RCT found that a noninvasive method of collecting clean-catch urine was effective within 5 minutes 31% of the time compared to control group which consisted of waiting for the infant to urinate (12%; p <0.001): Clean the genital area and then rub the suprapubic area in a circular motion with a gauze soaked in cold normal saline. Contamination occured in 27% of samples.

If a clinician decides that a febrile infant (2-24 months) with no apparent source for fever requires antibiotics (eg, ill appearing), a urine specimen for culture and urinalysis should be obtained (via SPA or transurethral catheterization) prior to initiating antibiotics.

If a clinician decides that a febrile infant (2-24 months) with no apparent source for fever does not require immediate antibiotics, then testing for UTI can be based on likelihood of UTI. Febrile infants with a low likelihood for UTI can be monitored with clinical follow-up without testing.

Febrile infants not in the low-risk group should have either (1) urine culture and urinalysis on urine obtained via SPA or catheterization or (2) urinalysis of fresh urine (<1 hour since void at room temperature or <4 hours after void with refrigeration) obtained via urine bag with urine culture obtained via SPA or catheterization if urinalysis suggests a UTI (positive leukocyte esterase, positive nitrite, or microscopic analysis with leukocytes or bacteria).

There is a low likelihood of concomitant bacterial meningitis in infants 29 to 90 days of age diagnosed with UTI through positive urinalysis or positive urine culture (frequency of concomitant bacterial meningitis is 0.25%, 95% CI: 0.09%-0.70%).
Positive dipstick for both LE and nitrite is most accurate for ruling in disease. Positive microscopy for both pyuria and bacteriuria is most useful to rule in disease.
Negative dipstick for both LE and nitrite and microscopic analysis negative for both pyuria and bacteriuriamay be used to rule out the disease.

A study identified 300 children with acute suspected UTI in the primary care setting. In comparison with urine culture, Uriscreen, Rapidbac, and Utriplex point of care tests, as well as either LE or nitrite positive on dipstick were compared. Uriscreen was most sensitive (67%) and Utriplex was most specific (94%), but all had only modest accuracy (LR+ range 2.2 to 3.5, LR- range 0.5 to 0.8).

In febrile infants aged 2-6 months, a urine dipstick (positive nitrite or leukocyte esterase greater than or equal to 1+) had higher diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity 90.2%, specificity 92.6%) than urinalysis for UTI, with a negative predictive value of 98.6% in a population with 11.1% prevalence.

Diagnosis of UTI requires both a urinalysis that suggests infection (pyuria and/or bacteriuria) and at least 50,000 cfu/ml of a uropathogen on urine culture obtained through clean catch, SPA, or catheterization.

The presence of >5 squamous epithelial cells on urinalysis may indicate a higher likelihood of contamination, as evidenced by growth of fewer than 104 CFUs pathogenic organisms, mixed growth of multiple bacterial species in any concentration, or any growth of nonpathogenic organisms on urine culture from the same sample.

A study found that optimal cutoffs for diagnosing UTI in children <24 months varied with urine concentration (classified as low <1.011, moderate 1.011-1.020, and high >1.020); the cutoffs were 3, 5 and 8 WBC/HPF respectively.

listitem.strong: Other tests: Gram Stain and PCR

list.listitem: Urine gram stain and dipstick urine for nitrites combined with leukocyte preparation are equal in detecting UTI and are better than pyuria on urine microscopy.
UTI diagnosis requires positive urinalysis (pyuria and/or bacteruria) and a positive urine culture (>50,000 cfu/ml of a uropathogen).
A prospective cohort study found that urine PCR has a high sensitivity and specificity for E.coli UTI in children.
Renal and bladder ultrasound is recommended for febrile children less than 24 months of age with UTI.

The primary goal of radiologic workup is to identify structural abnormalities that could benefit from surgery. About 1% to 2% of ultrasounds performed after the first UTI show abnormalities that are potentially correctable through surgery.

VCUG should not be performed routinely after the first febrile UTI in infants 2 to 24 months.VCUG should be performed in children with (1) abnormal renal ultrasound (eg, hydronephrosis, scarring, or other findings indicating obstructive uropathy or high-grade vesicoureteral reflux) or (2) recurrent febrile UTIs.
A clinical rule has been developed to predict likelihood of UTI in girls under the age of 2 years presenting with fever.
The following five factors that predicted UTI were identified: age less than 12 months, temperature higher than 39°C, white race, fever for 2 days or more, and no other potential source of fever.

Risk of UTI was 5% overall; 0.8% if none or one of those factors is present; 6.5% if two or more factors are present; 11.4% if 3 or more factors are present; 33% if 4 or more factors are present; 45% if 5 risk factors are present. The rule has been retrospectively validated, but not prospectively validated, however.

A clinical decision rule was developed for identifying which children <5 years old should have their urine tested for UTI. Dysuria, smelly urine, absence of severe cough, severe illness, and prior UTI helped identify which children should be tested for UTI. Children with 5 or more points (2 points for each positive sign/symptom, only 1 point for history of prior UTI) had a AUROC 0.86 (52% sensitive, 95% specific). The prediction model needs to be prospectively validated.

Primary initial oral outpatient antibiotic choices are cefixime, cephalexin, and sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim; alternatives are nitrofurantoin and ciprofloxacin (age permitting) with choice guided by local resistance patterns. B
IV antibiotic choices include cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, gentamicin, tobramycin, and piperacillin. B

Hospitalize infants younger than 1 month of age and infants and children who need IV fluids or IV antibiotics due to severe illness, lack of response to PO antibiotics, or when family is uncomfortable with outpatient treatment. C
Consult a pediatric urologist if renal calculi are suspected, if VUR is present, or if renal scarring or other anatomic abnormality exists. C

Primary initial oral outpatient antibiotic choices are cefixime, cephalexin, cefuroxime, cefprozil, cefpodoxime, amoxicillin/clavulanate, sulfisoxazole and sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for 7 to 14 days. Alternative medicines are nitrofurantoin and ciprofloxacin (depending on age). More resistance is encountered with amoxicillin.
Resistance to a certain antibiotic differs among hospitals or regions. Initial choice of antibiotics depends on resistance data and child's age while awaiting culture and sensitivity results.

IV antibiotics should be considered for children with suspected UTI who have a toxic appearance and are dehydrated or vomiting. IV antibiotic choices include cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, gentamicin, tobramycin, and piperacillin.
IV antibiotics should be continued until the patient is afebrile for 12 hours and can tolerate PO antibiotics.
Oral antibiotics or a 2 to 4 day course of IV antibiotics followed by oral antibiotics are effective for treatment of pyelonephritis in children.
Refer to the algorithms in and for the diagnostic and treatment approaches toward UTI in children.
Surgical treatment is effective for severe VUR (grades 4 and 5) and for lower grades with progressive scarring on medical treatment.
A meta-analysis of controlled trials showed that antibiotics should be administered for 7 to 14 days for febrile UTIs. This resulted in fewer treatment failures compared with shorter courses.
A Cochrane review showed that a 4-day antibiotic course may be as effective as a longer course for lower UTI (cystitis).
Hospitalize and administer IV antibiotics to all infants younger than 1 month of age.
Hospitalize infants and children who need IV fluids or IV antibiotics due to severe illness, lack of response to PO antibiotics, or when family is uncomfortable with outpatient treatment.

Consult with a pediatric urologist if renal calculi are suspected or if VUR, renal scarring, or other anatomic abnormalities are present. Grades 1 and 2 VUR tend to resolve or improve with time; hence consultation depends on the physician's comfort with management.
Give IV antibiotics and hydration.
Child may be discharged if afebrile for 12 hours and can tolerate PO antibiotics.
Recurrent UTI can recur within the first 6 months of the initial treated episode. C
Untreated pyelonephritis may result in permanent renal damage and scarring. C
Aggressive treatment will decrease the incidence of hypertension and renal scarring. B
Untreated pyelonephritis may result in permanent renal damage and scarring.
Recurrent UTI can occur within the first 6 months of the initial treated episode.
Aggressive treatment will decrease the incidence of hypertension and renal scarring.
Urine culture obtained before treatment should be checked within 48 to 72 hours and antibiotics adjusted accordingly.

No evidence that antibiotic prophylaxis is effective in preventing recurrent febrile UTI in children with vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). However, only 5 children included in the RCTs had Grade V VUR. A 2-year RCT of 607 children with VUR found that antibiotic prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prevented recurrent UTIs by 50% (HR: 0.50; 95% CI: 0.34-0.74), and was particularly effective in children whose index UTI was a febrile UTI (HR: 0.41; 95% CI: 0.26-0.64) and in those with baseline bladder and bowel dysfunction (HR: 0.21; 95% CI: 0.08-0.58). There was no difference in occurence of renal scarring.

A meta-analysis of 7 RCTs involving 1427 children with symptomatic or febrile UTIs found that antibiotic prophylaxis did not prevent renal scarring (pooled risk ratio: 0.83; 95% CI: 0.55-1.26). However, there were few children with renal dysplasia or high grade vesicoureteral reflux in the studies.

After confirmation of the first febrile UTI, parents should be instructed to seek prompt medical evaluation (within 48 hours) for future febrile illnesses as early treatment limits renal damage and the risk of renal scarring increases with recurrent febrile UTIs.
Scheduled bathroom use every 2 to 3 hours may help decrease recurrence and renal scarring, especially in children with voiding dysfunction.
Avoid constipation and increase dietary fiber.
